abstract: Theoretical paper proposing a nested CES production function with three capital types (traditional capital, industrial robots, AI). Industrial robots predominantly substitute for low-skill workers while AI mainly performs tasks of high-skill workers; under this structure, AI reduces the skill premium as long as it is more substitutable for high-skill workers than low-skill workers are for high-skill workers.
keyFindings: AI reduces the skill premium as long as it is more substitutable for high-skill workers than low-skill workers are for high-skill workers.
Numerical illustration: baseline skill premium of about 2 (high-skill wages twice low-skill wages).
When AI capital reaches half the industrial-robot stock, the skill premium decreases to about 1.7.
When AI capital equals the robot stock, the skill premium shrinks to 1.62.
Use of AI is neutral for the skill premium only if AI is equally substitutable for high- and low-skill workers.
methodology: Nested constant elasticity of substitution (CES) production function with three capital types; comparative statics plus numerical simulation with calibrated parameters. NBER Working Paper 32430, May 2024. Theoretical model, not an empirical estimate.
qualifiers: Model-based simulation, not observed wage data. Skill premium defined as high-skill over low-skill wages, which differs from the site's high-skill-over-median metric - hence classified as a directional overlay rather than a data point.
